samples.summary: `files download` falls back to the raw, unsanitized `docId` as the output filename, allowing an arbitrary-path file create outside the CWD
samples.evidence: `resolveDownloadTarget` deliberately reduces the *server-supplied* Content-Disposition name to a bare filename (`basename(serverName)`, line 26) and even rejects `.`/`..` — but when that name is absent it returns `docId` verbatim (line 27) with no `basename`, no dot-segment rejection. `docId` reaches this function straight from argv (`commands/files.ts:67`, `{ docId, out, ... }`) and, in the agent workflow this CLI is built for, is typically copied out of a `docs list` / `files list` response, i.e. it is server-controlled. Vector: a hostile or compromised backend lists a document whose `id` is `../../../../home/user/.config/autostart/x.desktop`; the agent runs `wafflebase files download <id>` with no `--out`; the request is sent (percent-encoded, so it reaches the malicious server fine), the server answers 200 with bytes and omits `Content-Disposition`, and `writeBinary` → `defaultBinaryIO.writeFile` (`output/binary.ts:63`) creates that path with the `wx` flag. `wx` only blocks *overwriting* an existing file — creating a new file anywhere the user can write succeeds, and `--force` removes even that limit. The file's own doc comment claims a title of `../../.bashrc` "must not decide where the CLI writes", which holds for the Content-Disposition branch but not for the fallback.

samples.summary: `safeEnvelope`'s content bounds are trivially bypassable: only `code` and `message` are clamped, every other upstream-controlled field is spread through unchecked
samples.evidence: `safeEnvelope` builds `const error = { ...body.error, code }` (line 163) and `const whole = { ...body, error }` (line 167). Only `error.code` (80 chars) and `error.message` (500 chars, HTML rejected) are sanitized; any sibling the upstream chose to attach — `error.detail`, `error.hint`, a top-level `stack` — passes through with no length cap, no HTML rejection, and only the aggregate 4 000-char budget. So the stated policy ("a stack trace or a megabyte of debug context is not" kept, lines 100-104) is defeated by renaming the field: an upstream that returns `{error:{code:'X',message:'m',detail:'<3.9 KB of anything>'}}` gets all 3.9 KB printed verbatim to the agent's stderr, including HTML the `message` path explicitly refuses. The budget is also measured on `JSON.stringify(whole)` (compact) while the output is `JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)` (pretty), so the actual bytes emitted exceed the documented 4 KB cap. This is a weakness in the sanitizer this diff introduces, not in the code it replaced.

samples.summary: `assertNoDotSegments` implements a weaker dot-segment test than the URL parser it is defending against (misses `%2e` forms) and stops scanning at the first `?`
samples.evidence: The comment on lines 15-18 sells this as the invariant guarding a raw id that reached the preview builder unencoded. But WHATWG URL treats a segment as a double-dot segment when it is `..` **or** an ASCII case-insensitive match for `.%2e`, `%2e.`, `%2e%2e` (and single-dot for `.` or `%2e`), while the check on line 48 compares only against the literal `'.'` and `'..'`. It also discards everything after the first `?` (line 47), so a raw id containing `?` followed by `../..` is never inspected. A raw id of `%2e%2e/%2e%2e/workspaces/other/api-keys` would therefore be printed as "the request that would be sent" and, when the agent pastes that URL into curl/a browser, normalizes out of the workspace base — precisely the outcome the guard exists to prevent. No current caller passes a raw id (every `printDryRun` site seg()s first, verified across cells.ts, tabs.ts, docs.ts, notes.ts, slides.ts, files.ts, sheets-import.ts), so this is a defence-in-depth gap rather than a live exploit — but a guard that reads as covering the case and does not is the failure mode the diff itself warns about.

samples.summary: `seg()` accepts the empty string, emitting an empty path segment that a normalizing proxy can collapse into a different endpoint
samples.evidence: `seg('')` returns `''`, so an unset workspace (`resolveConfig` defaults `workspace` to `''` in all four branches, config.ts:100/126/147/164) yields `${server}/api/v1/workspaces//documents`. Node's fetch preserves the empty segment, but many reverse proxies and gateways (nginx `merge_slashes on` by default) collapse `//` before routing, so the request that arrives is `/api/v1/workspaces/documents` — a different route than the CLI named, sent with the session bearer token. The same applies to an empty document/tab id. Since `seg()` is the one place that decides what a legal segment is, and it already refuses `.`/`..`, refusing `''` belongs there too. Low confidence: I could not confirm a deployment that merges slashes, and the empty-workspace case is pre-existing (see the comment at config.ts:107-110).

samples.summary: The id-escapes-its-segment fix was applied only to the CLI; the credentialed frontend API client still interpolates route-param ids into request paths unencoded
samples.evidence: This change establishes the rule (docs/design/cli.md §10: "Ids are one path segment each") and enforces it in `HttpClient`/`printDryRun`. The frontend client, which talks to the same API with the user's session via `fetchWithAuth`, has the identical unencoded pattern and no `seg()` equivalent: `documents.ts:46` (`GET /documents/${id}`), `:64`/`:87` (PATCH), `:109` (POST copy), `:154` (DELETE), plus `share-links.ts:60/78`, `files.ts:22`, `analytics.ts:127`. The ids come from `useParams()` (e.g. `notes-detail.tsx:213` → `fetchDocument(id!)`, `board-detail.tsx:140`), and react-router hands the param back percent-decoded, so a link of the form `/n/%2E%2E%2F%2E%2E%2F<other-endpoint>` yields `id = '../../<other-endpoint>'`, which `fetch` resolves — issuing the component's own method (GET on mount, DELETE/PATCH on a user action) against an endpoint the app never named, with the victim's credentials. Confidence low because I did not confirm the route pattern accepts a slash-bearing param end-to-end or find a high-impact target endpoint; the vector class is the same one the diff fixes on the CLI side.

samples.summary: SSRF: `docs export` / `slides export` fetch arbitrary absolute URLs taken from document content with no scheme or host restriction
samples.evidence: `resolveImageUrl` passes through any value matching `/^[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*:/i` untouched (line 28) and `createImageFetcher` fetches it (line 49), with the resolved URL echoed into the error message on failure (line 52). The `src` comes from the document body — content another workspace member, a shared doc, or an agent authored — so `wafflebase docs export <id> out.pdf` will GET e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/...` or `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` from the operator's machine and embed the response bytes into the exported PDF/DOCX, which is commonly shared back. No allowlist, no loopback/link-local rejection, no redirect limit. Pre-existing and untouched by this diff; raised here because it is the same 'untrusted content decides which URL we request' class the change is otherwise closing, and nothing in the enforced lanes covers it. Confidence low on exploitability (I did not verify a deployment where an attacker can plant an image inline in a doc the victim exports).

samples.summary: Upstream-controlled error text is now quoted into the agent's stderr at ~40 additional call sites that previously emitted only `HTTP <status>`
samples.evidence: `upstreamMessage` (line 176) splices up to 500 characters of the response body's `message` into the envelope, and `forwardUpstreamError` now backs every `!res.ok` branch in the CLI — the ~25 sites converted from `throw new Error("HTTP ${res.status}")` previously discarded that text entirely. The CLI's stated purpose is to be read by an LLM agent (README "Skills (for AI agents)"), so this newly routes server-controlled prose into an agent's context on every failing request, which is a prompt-injection surface. JSON.stringify neutralizes ANSI/control bytes, and the ergonomic argument for keeping the message is sound, so this is hardening rather than a break — but the widened exposure is a deliberate consequence of the change and worth an explicit decision (e.g. character-class restriction on forwarded text). Low confidence: I could not identify a backend path where one user's input is echoed into another user's error body (the interpolated exceptions I found — analytics.controller.ts:113, image.service.ts:100 — echo the caller's own input).

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. resolveDownloadTarget (packages/cli/src/files/download.ts:25-28) sanitizes the server-supplied Content-Disposition name with basename() and rejects '.'/'..', but its fallback (line 27) returns the raw `docId` with no basename, no dot-segment rejection, and no containment check. That value flows unmodified to writeBinary (download.ts:61-62) -> defaultBinaryIO.writeFile -> writeFileSync(path, bytes, {flag: force ? 'w' : 'wx'}) (output/binary.ts:38, 63). The 'wx' flag only prevents overwriting an existing file; creating a NEW file at an arbitrary relative or absolute path (e.g. ../../../../home/user/.config/autostart/x.desktop) succeeds, and --force (commands/files.ts:58) downgrades to 'w', permitting overwrite too. I searched for a guard on the path and found none: the only id validation is seg() (client/url.ts:24-29), which throws only on the exact strings '.' and '..' and otherwise percent-encodes, so a traversal-bearing docId passes through as a single URL segment and a hostile/compromised backend can answer 200 with bytes and no Content-Disposition, driving the fallback. http-client.ts:269-273 adds no docId validation. docId reaches the function straight from argv (commands/files.ts:59-68). The repo's own threat model in url.ts:4-6 explicitly treats ids as untrusted ("arrives from argv, a config file or a document an agent generated"), so this is not a trusted-argv case; it is in-lane path traversal / arbitrary file write. Existing tests (test/files-download.test.ts:84-87) confirm the unsanitized fallback is the intended, exercised behavior rather than dead code. No refutation ground applies.

The URL originates from untrusted document content: docs.ts:251-263 and slides.ts:207-210 build this fetcher and pass it into exporters that call it with inline image `src` values straight from the fetched document (docx-exporter.ts:425-433, pdf-image-painter.ts:56-59, slides/export/pdf.ts:282), embedding the response bytes into the exported artifact. finding.summary: `--dry-run` bypasses the new one-segment encoding and the `.`/`..` refusal, printing a traversal URL as "the request that would be sent"
finding.evidence:
The delta documents (docs/design/cli.md §10 additions) that every id the client interpolates is percent-encoded by `seg()` and that a `.`/`..` id is refused with exit 1 "before any request is sent". That guarantee lives only in `HttpClient` (packages/cli/src/client/http-client.ts:71-76). The second, parallel URL builder — `printDryRun` (packages/cli/src/client/dry-run.ts:13) — interpolates `config.workspace` and the caller-built `path` raw:

  const url = `${server}/api/v1/workspaces/${config.workspace}${path}`;

and every command builds that `path` from raw argv ids and returns *before* the client is ever touched: `packages/cli/src/commands/cells.ts:52-58` (`/documents/${docId}/tabs/${tab}/cells/${ref}`), `cells.ts:85-90`, `cells.ts:133-139`, `tabs.ts:48`, `tabs.ts:72`, `sheets-import.ts:84`, `notes.ts:94`, `notes.ts:112`, `notes.ts:140`, `files.ts:63`, `files.ts:123`, `files.ts:141`, `docs.ts:134`.

Attack/exposure: `wafflebase sheets cells set '../../../../workspaces/other-ws/api-keys/key-1' A1 x --dry-run` exits 0 and prints `"url": "https://api…/api/v1/workspaces/ws-1/documents/../../../../workspaces/other-ws/api-keys/key-1/tabs/…"`, and `--workspace ..` / a doc id of `..` is likewise not refused here (no `seg()` call in this file at all). docs/design/cli.md:815-826 promises dry-run "prints the request that would be sent", and the CLI is explicitly aimed at agents (docs/design/cli.md:22-26), which are the consumers most likely to take the printed URL and run it through `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer …"` — executing exactly the out-of-base request, with the session's bearer token and the command's method, that `seg()` was added to prevent. Even absent that, the preview now misreports the request: the real send would either 404 on an escaped literal id or throw `Invalid path segment`.

Fix is one line: route the dry-run URL through the same `seg()` (export it) so preview and send agree, and so the dot-segment refusal fires on the dry-run path too.

verdict.reason: The code is not as described. `printDryRun` does NOT interpolate raw values: packages/cli/src/client/dry-run.ts:2 imports `seg`, line 29 builds the URL with `seg(config.workspace)` (so `--workspace ..` throws), and line 26 calls `assertNoDotSegments(path)` (defined lines 44-52), which raises `seg()`'s own `Invalid path segment` error for any `.`/`..` segment of the previewed path — the exact refusal the finding says is absent. The claim "no seg() call in this file at all" is false. Every command dry-run branch the finding cites also wraps ids in `seg()`, not raw argv: cells.ts:56, cells.ts:89, cells.ts:137; tabs.ts:52, tabs.ts:81; sheets-import.ts:88; notes.ts:95,115,146,201; files.ts:64,124,144; docs.ts:135,155,191,246; slides.ts:100,120,152,203. I enumerated all 24 `printDryRun(` call sites (cells 3, tabs 2, sheets-import 1, notes 5, files 3, slides 5, docs 5); every id-bearing path uses `seg()` and the rest are constant `'/documents'` paths. The claimed exploit output is directly contradicted by packages/cli/test/dry-run.test.ts:33-34, which asserts the traversal id prints percent-encoded (`..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fworkspaces%2Fother-ws%2Fapi-keys%2Fkey-1`) and drives the dot-segment refusal through the real command. Preview and send therefore agree; there is no traversal URL printed and no bypass of the dot-segment refusal.
